1.pericope_label: Remember the way: the forty years of humbling, proving, and the manna

schools.summary: Deny that the opening verse is a bare promise of reward, since Moses sets before them the previous favour with which God had gratuitously prevented them, and reads the commandments as handed down from God's own mouth rather than invented; and make the manna a rebuke to ordinary religious perception, which ties itself to meat and drink, binds God to outward instruments, and holds the knowledge of his providence as a cold notion that speedily vanishes.

Ask whether the first verse closes the preceding paragraph, and take possession of the land to mean the detailed work left after the first conquest; explain the forty years as the humbling by which God proved the state of their heart, or as the probation without which the formation of character would vanish; and deny that what proceeds from the mouth of the Lord is the word of the law, while noticing that the manna was withheld a full month and that our Lord fasted a day for each year of the Exodus.

Draw from the charge that obedience must be careful, universal and from a good principle, with reverence of God's majesty and dread of his wrath, and figure the wilderness as the school in which Israel was boarded and taught through its minority, now recalled as they come of age to their inheritance.

Make the proving a discovery Israel needed to make about itself rather than one God needed to make, useful to the church in every age since; take every word to mean whatever God appoints, however unlikely, since the blessing and not the creature sustains life; and hold that no tribulation is permitted which is not designed to turn to advantage.

debates: Whether the promise attached to obedience is a reward offered or a prior grace recalled.
Whether the forty years proved Israel for God's knowledge, for their own self-knowledge, or as the training without which character could not be formed.
What is meant by every word that proceeds out of the mouth of the Lord — the law, the secret power of God, or whatever means he appoints.
What the humbling consisted in: hunger alone, or the unfamiliar food that answered it.
outliers: Calvin alone argues that the verse would be misread as a promise and reclassifies it as an appeal to gratitude.
Keil alone names and rejects a rabbinic reading of the phrase about the mouth of the Lord.
Ellicott alone matches the forty days of the temptation to the forty years, a day for a year.
Ellicott alone computes how long the people went before the manna began, and how long it then continued.
Wesley alone makes the proving a disclosure to Israel about itself rather than a test before God.

4.pericope_label: The raiment that waxed not old, and the chastening of a son

schools.summary: Read the unworn clothing naturally — a well-supplied people with weavers and traders and their own flocks — and price the miraculous reading as a chain of continual miracles wrought on every thread, since garments would have to grow with six hundred thousand children and shrink again for the next; and take the figure of the chastening father as a set of limits, that he corrects unwillingly, moderately, and for reformation rather than destruction.

Rehearse the Jewish explanations of how Israel was clothed and then insist that the clothes not wearing out is miraculous whatever the supply; object that the verb for chastening is taken too narrowly when read as punishment, since it covers the whole process of a proper education; and find in raiment that never wears out the everlasting righteousness of Christ.

Resist the naturalising reading from the vocabulary, the verb meaning to fall off through age and the rare word for the foot being of doubtful sense, and hold that the clause says more than that clothes and shoes never failed; or else allow that nothing miraculous is certainly meant, and take the chastening as proof of love rather than method, since training implies time and the Lord chastens whom he loves.

debates: Whether the raiment that waxed not old requires a miracle, an ample natural provision, or neither with certainty.
What the rare verb used of the foot means, and how much the clause affirms beyond the sufficiency of supplies.
Whether the word for chastening means punishment or the whole work of education.
Whether the point of the fatherly comparison is the love that prompts the discipline or the restraint that governs it.
outliers: Clarke alone computes the cost of the miracle in threads and particles, and in the wardrobes of six hundred thousand growing children.
Gill alone reports the argument that manna produced no sweat and so spared the clothes.
Keil alone appeals to the sole parallel occurrence of the word in Nehemiah and to the Septuagint's two different renderings of it.
Wesley alone reads the fatherly analogy as limiting God to chastening unwillingly and in measure.
Keil cites Calvin by name on the breadth of the word for chastening, so that the two schools agree here by transmission rather than independently.

7.pericope_label: The good land: its waters, its produce, its iron and brass

schools.summary: Read the description as an argument for gratitude rather than an inventory, and make the manner of watering decisive — Egypt is irrigated by drains and human industry, Canaan waits for rain from heaven — while conceding that no corner of the earth lacks God's blessing; press the clause about the land being looked on all the year as requiring a constant answering regard; and supply the plenty from Solomon's household, the grain sent to Hiram and the wheat sold at Tyre.

Set the land term by term against the desert it replaces, and correct the rendering so that the fountains go forth in the valley and on the hill; hold that the desolation of Palestine now proves the divine word as much as its former beauty did; and grant that brass means copper and that sacred history records no mining there, whatever the iron in the stones.

Deny that there is any such thing as a brass mine and render the word copper; or else read the iron as lying about the surface in such quantity that travellers tread on it; and fill out the list of fruits from a traveller's observations of olives, figs and the pomegranates used for cooling drinks.

debates: Why the manner of the land's watering matters, and what it teaches about dependence.
Whether the present desolation of the land tells against the description or confirms the word that gave it.
Whether the metal named is brass or copper, and whether Israel mined at all.
Whether the promised plenty is to be established from later scripture, from travellers, or from the terms of the description itself.
outliers: Ellicott alone turns the ruin of the country into evidence for the truth of the text that praised it.
Calvin alone rests the theology of the passage on irrigation, distinguishing a fruitfulness men can credit to their own industry from one they cannot.
Wesley alone escapes the mining difficulty by making the iron lie on the surface.
Clarke alone answers a verse about produce almost entirely by quoting a traveller, and ends on the bee-keeping of Egypt.
Gill alone names the towns the Jewish writers reckoned best for fine flour.

10.pericope_label: Bless the Lord when thou art full: the duty of plenty and the danger in it

schools.summary: Attach rules to the blessing after meat — not to eat so much as to be unfit for it, to keep no company with those who bless false gods when full, and to give God the glory of whatever one has the comfort of — and note that scripture teaches a blessing after the meal where the Saviour taught one before it.

Cite the rabbinic saying that no enjoyment may be taken from this world without thanksgiving; observe that the whole warning is one sentence in the Hebrew and set out its clauses; call the caution prophetic and name the kings whose hearts were lifted up when they grew strong; and trace the chain from plenty through the lifted heart to wealth ascribed to one's own hand.

Treat the failure to acknowledge the giver as unreasonable rather than merely unlawful, and diagnose prosperity as an intoxicant in which scarcely one man in a hundred escapes headiness; identify pride as the cause, since men admire their own exaltation until they despise God, and warn that uninterrupted prosperity corrupts even the best by degrees, so that watch must be kept through a whole life and not for a day.
Call the praise a debt of justice as well as gratitude, and rebuke those who profess to believe in the God from whom their comforts come and yet grudge to own him at their meals.

debates: Whether thanksgiving after eating is a matter of law, of reason, or of justice owed.
How the warning against forgetting God is constructed, and what its single Hebrew sentence governs.
Whether the caution is general counsel or a prophecy of particular failures later recorded.
Why plenty produces forgetfulness when it ought to produce remembrance.
outliers: Ellicott alone reads the passage as a single sentence and reconstructs its clauses accordingly.
Ellicott alone names three kings in whom the warning was afterwards fulfilled.
Henry alone forbids eating so much as to be unfit for the thanksgiving that follows.
Calvin alone puts a figure on the failure, that scarcely one in a hundred escapes.
Ellicott alone sets the Rechabite vow to live in tents against the goodly houses of the warning.

13.pericope_label: The lifted heart, the terrible wilderness, and why God let them hunger

schools.summary: Fix the wilderness geographically and describe the scorpion from Pliny and Aristotle; and make the hunger a lesson in perception — the people must have perished had God not made the rock run and sent bread from heaven, the trial exposed their incredulity while his goodness pardoned it, and had they never gone hungry the daily supply would have passed unnoticed, since abundance veils the eyes and want purges the dimness away.

Expand the boast of the lifted heart to cover merit as well as ability; describe the bite of the fiery serpents by its symptoms; and argue that daily dependence proves a man helpless, then turn the argument round — mercies humble as powerfully as afflictions, because they increase our debts and by making God great make us little in our own eyes.

Distinguish the word used of the rock at Horeb, which conveys hardness, from the word used of the rock at Kadesh, which suggests a cliff and inaccessibility, while admitting that the purpose of the distinction cannot be stated; and collect the other occurrences of the term for flint.

debates: Whether the boast of the lifted heart claims ability only or also desert.
Which rock is meant and what the change of word between the two occasions signifies.
Why God let the people hunger before he fed them.
Whether mercy or affliction is the more effective means of humbling.
outliers: Wesley alone adds merit to the wisdom, valour and industry the proud heart claims.
Ellicott alone distinguishes the two Hebrew words for rock and then concedes he cannot say why they differ.
Calvin alone makes abundance a veil over the eyes and want the thing that purges the sight.
Wesley alone argues that mercies humble as powerfully as afflictions do.
Gill alone calls the scorpion a kind of serpent and supports it from Pliny and Aristotle.

17.pericope_label: My power and the might of mine hand: the boast answered and the warning closed

schools.summary: Name the boast as the principal form of pride, since it assigns to ourselves what belongs to God, and locate the fault in the heart rather than the lips, where profession is often only hypocrisy; recall the manna as standing proof that life is sustained by the secret power of God; and read the threat against Israel as exactly the judgment being executed on the nations before them, noting that the Targum's Word of the Lord is Christ.

Turn the counter-statement into a series of questions — who gives wisdom, skill, strength, health, fertility and a right issue to our purposes, and how is wealth acquired without them — and conclude that since God gives the power to get wealth, the wealthy man must account to him for the way he has spent it.

Render the closing clause as in return for your disobedience, and observe that the same word stands at the head of the preceding section, so that the repetition may mark off everything between as one complete portion of the discourse.

debates: Whether the pride the chapter warns against is one fault among many or the root of them all.
Whether the required acknowledgment is a profession of the lips or a settled persuasion of the heart.
What follows from the confession that God gives the power to get wealth.
Where this section of the discourse begins and ends.
outliers: Clarke alone draws an obligation of account from the verse, making the giver of wealth its auditor.
Calvin alone dismisses the outward profession of gratitude as commonly hypocrisy and vanity.
Gill alone reads the voice of the Lord through the Targum as the personal Word, and identifies him with Christ.
Ellicott alone argues from a repeated word that the passage is a bounded section, having also questioned at the outset where the chapter begins.
